data.title: Administrative Interface Exposed to Untrusted Networks
data.summary: Administrative and remote-access interfaces were reachable from untrusted networks, placing authentication for high-value services directly in front of anyone who can route to them.
data.description:
Management interfaces assume a trusted network. Exposing them to the internet, or to a general user subnet, removes that assumption while keeping the design decisions that depended on it: permissive defaults, legacy authentication, and slow patch cycles.

Exposed RDP and SSH attract continuous credential attacks. Exposed hypervisor, backup, and VPN appliance interfaces are of particular interest because a single flaw there is a path to the whole estate, and because these products have repeatedly carried pre-authentication vulnerabilities that are exploited within days of disclosure.

The exposure is often unintentional — a firewall rule added for a migration, a cloud security group opened for troubleshooting, or an appliance that listens on all interfaces by default.
data.recommendation:
* Place management interfaces on a dedicated network reachable only through a bastion or a VPN requiring multi-factor authentication.
* Review perimeter rules against an inventory of what is intentionally published, and remove temporary rules on a schedule.
* Require MFA for all administrative access.
* Monitor the external attack surface continuously rather than at audit time.
data.short_recommendation: Restrict management interfaces to an administrative network.
